title: Photography direction for a law practice
metaTitle: Law practice website photography with a point
excerpt: Law practice website photography should show the kind of matter you take. Marble, Latin, and stock courthouses argue for a costume, not the work.
alt: A close view of a fountain pen writing on lined paper, the kind of specific work a practice should photograph instead of a marble costume.
caption: A pen on paper, which is closer to the work than a courthouse backdrop. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a law firm photograph for its website?
faqs.answer: Photograph the room where consultations happen, the people who do the featured work, and a staged document that is not a client file. Match the frames to the matters you want, such as leases or employment letters. A skyline or a stock courthouse does not show the job.

faqs.question: Why avoid marble textures and Latin mottos in photos?
faqs.answer: They reassure the firm and fail the client. A hurried person needs to see a real room and a real kind of matter. Marble and Latin look like every other serious costume, and they often cover the face or the sentence that would have helped.

faqs.question: How large should the hero image be?
faqs.answer: Export it at the size the page displays, and give it a known width and height so the layout does not jump. Google's Core Web Vitals guidance asks for Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds and Cumulative Layout Shift under 0.1. A carousel of textures spends that budget on decoration.

sources.title: Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results

markdown:
A law practice website photography plan should show the kind of matter you take. Choose pictures that make that matter easier to believe, and reject a marble texture and a line of Latin. The pictures are part of the argument. They are not a mood pasted under the headline.

A client choosing counsel under time pressure will judge the room, the person, and the paper before they finish the paragraph. Google's Core Web Vitals guidance treats the largest element in view, often a hero image, as a loading measure, and asks that Largest Contentful Paint occur within 2.5 seconds. A heavy marble photograph that arrives late has missed the moment the words needed it. Google's helpful-content guidance also asks for first-hand evidence. A courthouse you do not work in is not evidence.

## The picture has to argue for a matter

Decide the matter before you book a photographer. If the practice wants shop leases, the pictures should help a tenant imagine the review. A table, a printed draft, a pen, a person who looks like they read for a living. If the practice wants employment letters for small companies, show the kind of meeting where a founder brings a letter and leaves with a plan. If the practice is estates for family businesses, show a calm room where two generations could sit, not a courtroom drama.

One set of pictures should not pretend to cover every department. A single marble field behind twelve practice areas makes every area look like the same costume. Shoot for the matters you feature. The services page can use a tighter crop of the same session. The homepage can use the clearest frame, with the matter sentence beside it, not trapped in a dark overlay.

Write the argument in a sentence the photographer can read. "This frame should make a shop tenant believe we read leases in a real room." If you cannot write that sentence, you are still shopping for a mood. Moods are cheap, and they all look like the last firm that bought them.

People are allowed to be in the pictures. Name them, and only photograph staff who have agreed. A recognizable lawyer matched to a bio is worth more than a silhouette on a staircase. A client should be able to connect the about page to the face on the homepage without a guessing game.

## What to put on the shot list

A short shot list keeps the day honest. Bring it to the session. Do not improvise a brand out of whatever the light is doing.

- The consultation room in daylight, tidy, with real furniture. Include the table and the chairs a client will actually use.
- The lawyer who does the featured work, at that table, with a generic document that is not a client file. Blank paper and a printed public form are safer than a live matter.
- Hands marking a page, close enough to see that someone works on paper or on a screen, far enough that no name is readable.
- The entrance or the street, if the city is part of how clients sort you. One frame. Not a tourism reel.
- A detail that is true: the shelf, the notebook, the mug, the window. Specific beats luxurious.

Skip the gavel, the scale, the column, the handshake, the skyline from a stock library, and any Latin set in type across the sky. Those objects say "law" to a designer and "anyone" to a client. They do not say "we review shop leases."

If you need a document in frame, stage it. Use a lease from a public template, or a page of your own checklist with invented names removed. A real client's papers, even blurred, are a risk you do not need for a homepage. Tell the photographer that screens must be locked on a neutral page before the shutter goes.

Plan the crops before the shoot. You will need a wide frame for the hero, a tighter frame for a services block, and a face that still reads at the size of a phone. A beautiful horizontal that cannot be cropped without losing the person will force the mobile page to shrink the matter sentence. Shoot the vertical on purpose.

## Marble and Latin are a costume

Marble photographs reassure partners that the site looks serious. Serious, for this client, is a specific room and a specific job. The texture is the same one on hotels, banks, and the firm down the road. It does not sort a tenant from a landlord, or a small company from a multinational.

Latin fails in a picture the same way it fails in a headline. The client cannot read it at speed, and the letters often sit on top of the very face or room that would have helped. If the firm has a real inscription in the office, you can photograph it as architecture. Do not add a fake one in post.

Stock libraries make this worse because the same marble hall appears on competing sites. A client who has opened three firms in a lunch break will feel they have seen your building before. They have. It was never yours.

A calm, slightly plain room is a better argument. It looks like a place where someone could talk about a guarantee clause without performing. Hanabi's own public work leans on that kind of specificity. Down the Cove can show a store because the store is the product. Your product, in a photograph, is the room and the person who will read the file. Show those.

## Direction the photographer can follow

Give the photographer constraints, not adjectives. "Warm, premium, elevated" produces marble. Constraints produce the argument.

Name the people and the order. Who is photographed first, because they lead the featured matter. What they should wear, which is what they wear to a client meeting, not a costume from a catalogue. Whether they look at the page or at the camera. For a proof-of-work frame, the page is the point. For the about page, the face is the point. Shoot both.

Ban overlays in the session notes. No Latin, no scales composited in later, no dark gradient that exists only to make white type legible. If the type is hard to read, the photograph is too busy, or the type is in the wrong place. Move the type. Do not fog the room.

Ask for a contact sheet the same day, and choose frames against the sentence you wrote. Reject anything that could be a bank. Keep anything where a client could point and say "that is a lease review" or "that is the person from the bio."

Color should stay close to the room. A heavy grade that turns the office teal or gold is another costume. Natural color, moderate contrast, and enough brightness that a face is visible on a phone in daylight. If you design the page in Figma, place the real frames in the layout before you fall in love with a crop that breaks the headline.

Write alt text when you choose the frame, while you still remember what is in it. "A lawyer at a pale wooden table marking a blank lease, with a window behind her." That is alt text. "Best law firm image" is a keyword stuffed into a picture, and it fails the client who cannot see the screen.

## Speed is part of the picture

The hero image is a common Largest Contentful Paint element. Google's threshold for a good LCP is within 2.5 seconds of the page starting to load. Export the frame at the size the layout uses. A 6000-pixel original scaled down in the browser makes the client wait for marble they did not need.

Reserve the space. Cumulative Layout Shift should stay under 0.1, which means the image needs a known width and height so the text does not jump when the photograph arrives. A headline that moves while someone is trying to read the matter line is a self-inflicted miss during those first seconds.

Interaction to Next Paint should stay under 200 milliseconds. A carousel of eight atmospheres, with dots the thumb has to hunt, spends that budget on decoration. One still image, chosen for the matter, is faster and clearer. Motion that sweeps a texture across the hero is the same mistake in sequence.

Give the file a versioned name when you change it, so an old marble frame cannot linger in a cache and contradict the new sentence. The picture and the copy ship together.

## Where each frame goes

The homepage gets the single clearest argument, beside the matter and the consultation. Do not run a slideshow of every room.

The services page gets a crop that matches that service. Leases get the table and the paper. Employment advice gets the meeting. Do not reuse the courthouse on all of them to "keep it consistent." Consistency here is the shot list, the color, and the honesty. It is not one texture stamped everywhere.

The about page gets faces that match the names. The contact page gets the room they will enter, or the face of the person who replies, so the request feels like a continuation. Proof pages get an image of the decision, such as a staged markup, and never a confidential file.

Captions can carry a little of the argument. "The room where lease reviews happen." Alt text stays descriptive. The caption can be shorter than the alt text, and it should end by telling the truth about the source if the frame is not yours.

## Review the set before it goes live

Lay the chosen frames in order, without the rest of the design. Ask someone who is not on the partnership: what kind of matter does this firm take? If they say "expensive" or "old" or "law, I guess," the set is still a costume. If they say "they read leases" or "they sit with small companies," the pictures are doing the job.

Check the phone. The face or the page has to survive the crop. The matter sentence has to remain readable on top of, or beside, the frame. If the only way to read the sentence is to hide the photograph, you have the wrong frame or the wrong layout.

Then look at the first screen in motion, or rather the lack of it. The still should be enough. A client with a deadline does not need a slow pan across stone.

The next place the photograph fails is the phone layout itself. A desktop composition that looked balanced can push the matter and the consultation below the first screen once the image stacks. Read [how the mobile visit should work](/blog/the-mobile-visit-for-a-law-practice) before you approve a crop that only works on a wide monitor.

When you want to see photographs that stay specific to the work, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The useful test is whether the picture and the offer agree.
